kakekotoba.reading_primary: かけたる (to construct/build a weir, from 掛く)
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: かけたる (to hang/cast, as wind hanging leaves)
kakekotoba.interaction: The wind is described as having 'built/hung' (かけたる) the weir-like barrier of leaves — the verb simultaneously means the physical act of constructing a しがらみ (weir) and the more literal image of wind 'hanging' or 'casting' the leaves across the river, fusing the natural phenomenon (wind scattering leaves) with the artificial image of a man-made weir.

jokotoba.text: 山川に風のかけたるしがらみは
jokotoba.function: The entire kami-no-ku builds an elaborate conceit describing the wind as having constructed a weir (しがらみ) across the mountain river, which sets up the revelation in the shimo-no-ku that this apparent weir is in fact fallen autumn leaves caught in the current — the jokotoba functions less as a sound-based preface than as an extended metaphorical setup culminating in a visual revelation.

honkadori.source_poem: Kokinshū autumn poems on scattered leaves and weirs (topos of 紅葉のしがらみ)
honkadori.function: Draws on the established Kokinshū-era conceit of fallen leaves forming a 'weir' (しがらみ) in a mountain stream, a favorite autumn image of the era, reworking the topos with Tsuraki's own turn on wind as the builder of the weir.

kigo.note: 紅葉 (crimson/autumn leaves) is one of the most iconic autumn kigo in the classical canon, evoking the beauty and transience of the season; here it is the poem's climactic revelation — what seemed an artificial weir turns out to be nothing but drifting autumn leaves caught in the river's flow, the central image of autumnal transience and visual surprise.

bipartite.kami_theme: The wind has built a weir-like barrier (しがらみ) across the mountain river
bipartite.shimo_theme: What cannot flow away and be swept downstream turns out to be autumn leaves
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku presents what appears to be an artificial construction — a weir made by the wind — and the shimo-no-ku delivers the surprising visual truth: it is merely fallen crimson leaves unable to flow past, caught in the current. The poem's entire effect rests on this deferred revelation, a classic technique of describing an appearance before disclosing its true nature (nari-keri ending confirming the discovery).

source_jp:
山川に
風のかけたる
しがらみは
流れもあへぬ
紅葉なりけり
